Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process · [LLM] Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to the SharePoint endpoints abused by the July 2026 patch-Tuesday chain — /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx and the /_trust/default.aspx WS-Federation sign-in path where CVE-2026-50522 delivers a BinaryFormatter SecurityContextToken cookie. Surfaces the first foothold on internet-facing SharePoint servers. Rationale: Uses the two concrete exploit endpoints corroborated for this chain — ToolPane.aspx (CVE-2026-56164 EoP path) and /_trust/default.aspx (CVE-2026-50522 WS-Federation deserialization). Referer and low status codes help separate exploit probes from legit editing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authors editing web-part zones hit ToolPane.aspx from internal IPs
  • Federated SSO / ADFS traffic legitimately posting to /_trust/default.aspx
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable) probing SharePoint endpoints
  • Load-balancer / uptime monitors POSTing health checks
  • SharePoint farm timer jobs generating internal POSTs
Suppression filter
| where NOT (cidr_match("10.0.0.0/8", cIP) OR cidr_match("192.168.0.0/16", cIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the cIP is external/untrusted and correlate the timestamp with w3wp.exe child-process activity (UC2) on the same Computer. Pull the full csUriQuery and User-Agent. 2) Contain: block external access to SharePoint (as BIT did), and firewall the source IP; snapshot the server for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to any w3wp.exe→cmd/powershell spawns, reads of web.config/machine.config, and newly written .aspx files under the LAYOUTS directory in the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx", "/_trust/default.aspx") or csUriStem endswith "ToolPane.aspx"
| where scStatus in ("200","302","401","500")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE AIExploitation High
Alerts when the SharePoint/IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd.exe, powershell.exe or other interpreters/LOLBins. This parent→child chain is the execution signature of CVE-2026-50522 RCE and does not occur in normal SharePoint operation. Rationale: w3wp.exe (SharePoint app-pool worker) spawning an interpreter is the highest-fidelity execution signal for this chain — corroborated across Splunk, Trellix and Anomali ToolShell writeups as abnormal in legitimate SharePoint operation. Named parent/child binaries make it alert-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/sharepoint-exploits-and-the-hidden-threat-of-iis-module-persistence.html • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint installation/patching (PSConfig) transiently running under an app-pool identity
  • Admin-authored SharePoint timer jobs or custom web parts shelling out
  • Health-analyzer or monitoring solutions invoking scripts via the worker process
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation spawning under w3wp context
  • Custom in-house SharePoint solutions that legitimately call certutil/PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","wsadmin","stsadm") and InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel == "System")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any -EncodedCommand, look for download/machine-key strings. Correlate with UC1 inbound POSTs on the same host/time. 2) Contain: isolate the SharePoint server from the network and block external SharePoint access; suspend the app pool. Because machine keys may be stolen, plan key rotation + server reinstall (BIT reinstalled affected servers). 3) Hunt: search for web.config/machine.config reads (UC3), dropped .aspx webshells (UC4), and forged-token sign-ins across the ~200 potentially affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","csc.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\csc.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process AIInstallation High
Detects the credential-access step of CVE-2026-50522 where post-RCE code reads SharePoint ValidationKey/DecryptionKey material from web.config or machine.config to forge __VIEWSTATE/auth tokens. Fires on an interpreter spawned by w3wp.exe whose command line references machine-key config or key fields. Rationale: Targets the exact post-exploitation objective corroborated by BleepingComputer/HelpNetSecurity/watchTowr for CVE-2026-50522: stealing SharePoint machine keys (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey) from web.config/machine.config to forge tokens. The w3wp parent + key-material string combo is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patch/config operations (PSConfig, Update-SPMachineKey) legitimately touching machine keys
  • Admin PowerShell reading web.config for troubleshooting under the app-pool account
  • Farm build automation that rotates machine keys
  • Backup jobs enumerating config files
  • Custom deployment scripts referencing web.config paths
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Update-SPMachineKey","PSConfig") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and determine whether ValidationKey/DecryptionKey values were read or written out (base64/file redirection). Confirm the parent w3wp and any preceding UC1 POST. 2) Contain: treat machine keys as compromised — isolate the server, rotate/regenerate SharePoint machine keys across the farm, and force password resets on affected accounts (BIT reset ~200). 3) Hunt: because stolen keys enable forged tokens surviving patching, hunt for anomalous authenticated SharePoint sessions and __VIEWSTATE replays after the reset, and plan server reinstall.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the SharePoint worker process writing new .aspx/.ashx files into the SharePoint TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS or web-root directories — the webshell/key-exfil persistence pattern (e.g. spinstall0.aspx) used in the ToolShell chain to drop a page that returns the stolen machine keys or maintains RCE access. Rationale: The SharePoint worker writing a fresh .aspx into LAYOUTS (the spinstall0.aspx-style key-exfil/webshell drop documented in ToolShell) is a rare, high-signal persistence event that maps directly to this campaign's machine-key theft and post-patch access retention. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/on-prem-sharepoint-toolshell-backdoor-advisory/ • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patching/PSConfig deploying legitimate new LAYOUTS pages
  • Installation of a SharePoint solution package (WSP) that provisions .aspx files
  • Farm feature activation writing application pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in deployment
  • Developer publishing a custom application page during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","stsadm","Install-SPSolution"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the dropped .aspx — look for code that outputs ValidationKey/DecryptionKey, accepts commands, or reflects __VIEWSTATE. Note file hash and creation time; correlate with UC1/UC2/UC3. 2) Contain: remove/quarantine the file, isolate the server, and treat machine keys as stolen (rotate keys, reset affected account passwords, reinstall server per BIT's remediation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently-created .aspx/.ashx across the farm, check IIS logs for GETs to the dropped filename from external IPs, and review authenticated sessions for forged-token reuse post-patch.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\16\TEMPLATE", @"\web server extensions", @"\wwwroot")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS", "\\16\\TEMPLATE", "\\web server extensions", "\\wwwroot")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-56164", "CVE-2026-50522")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-56164", "CVE-2026-50522")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Zapscape KVM Flaw Could Let Privileged L1 Guest Code Escape to Linux Hosts

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 7 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Zapscape, a new Linux kernel vulnerability, could allow an attacker with kernel privileges inside an L1 guest virtual machine (VM) to escape KVM isolation and execute code on the host. The risk applies when nested virtualization is exposed to untrusted guests. The flaw is tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-64561&nbsp;and affects KVM/x86's shadow memory management unit (MMU), which manages shadow page

Zapscape KVM escape artifact: root-owned /Zapscape file created on host AIExploitation High
Hunts the definitive success marker of the Zapscape (CVE-2026-64561) KVM VM-escape PoC: a file literally named /Zapscape created at filesystem root, owned by root (uid=0, mode 0644), on a KVM hypervisor. Creation of this exact path by the host kernel confirms an L1 guest escaped shadow-MMU isolation and executed code with host root. Rationale: The PoC's own output string confirms it creates /Zapscape at root (uid=0, mode 0644) as its exploitation proof; a file with that exact name at filesystem root is not a legitimate artifact, making it a near-zero-FP success marker. Filename and behaviour cross-checked against the author's GitHub PoC (V4bel/Zapscape). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Zapscape • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-zapscape-kvm-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or red team running the public Zapscape PoC in a sanctioned lab
  • Blue team detonating the exploit to validate this very detection
  • A sysadmin manually running touch /Zapscape while testing the detection rule
  • Honeypot / deception host intentionally seeded with the marker file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("labadmin","secops-test") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the host is a KVM hypervisor exposing nested virtualization to guests; pull file owner/mode (expect root:root 0644) and the InitiatingProcess — a kernel/kworker context strongly implies genuine escape, a user shell implies manual/test creation. 2) Contain: Treat as full host compromise at kernel-root — isolate the hypervisor from the network, snapshot memory/disk for forensics, and quarantine/pause co-resident tenant VMs since any could be the origin guest. 3) Hunt: Identify the running kernel version vs fixed builds (6.6.148/6.12.101/6.18.42/7.1.6), review recent guest-side kernel module loads, and check for follow-on host root activity (new accounts, cron, SSH keys).

Exposure hunt: KVM hosts vulnerable to Zapscape (CVE-2026-64561) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces Linux hosts still carrying the Zapscape shadow-MMU use-after-free (CVE-2026-64561) so KVM hypervisors that expose nested virtualization to untrusted guests can be prioritised for patching to a fixed kernel (6.6.148, 6.12.101, 6.18.42, 7.1.6, or 7.2-rc5+). Article-specific exposure detection tied to the assigned CVE. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete CVE identifier (CVE-2026-64561) and enumerated fixed kernel versions to drive a targeted exposure hunt; joining to DeviceInfo flags internet-facing/multi-tenant hypervisors that carry the real escape risk. CVE and fixed versions corroborated against the PoC repo and vendor tracking. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Zapscape • https://cybernews.com/security/januscape-linux-kvm-vulnerability-exposes-cloud/
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but TVM inventory cache is stale (lag between patch and rescan)
  • Red Hat/vendor backported the fix without bumping the upstream version string, so version-string scanners may mis-flag a fixed host
  • Desktop/non-hypervisor Linux hosts where nested virt is not exposed to untrusted guests (vulnerable but low real-world risk)
  • VM guests rather than the KVM host itself appearing in results
Response runbook
1) Triage: Filter results to actual KVM hypervisors that expose nested virtualization to untrusted/multi-tenant guests — these are the true blast-radius hosts; deprioritise standalone desktops. 2) Contain: For internet-facing or multi-tenant hosts, schedule emergency patching to a fixed kernel (6.6.148/6.12.101/6.18.42/7.1.6/7.2-rc5+) or vendor backport; as interim mitigation, disable nested virtualization exposure to untrusted guests. 3) Hunt: On each exposed host, retro-hunt for the /Zapscape artifact and anomalous guest kernel-module loads to rule out prior exploitation before patch.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Traefik ReplacePathRegex path-traversal auth-bypass request (CVE-2026-65600) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Traefik reverse proxy whose path smuggles an implicit dot-segment immediately after a stripped prefix (e.g. GET /api../admin or the encoded /api%2e%2e/admin). This is the exact CVE-2026-65600 payload shape that selects the public no-auth router yet forwards an un-normalized /../admin to the backend, bypassing BasicAuth/ForwardAuth/DigestAuth. Rationale: Uses the article's two verbatim exploit shapes: the un-encoded `/api../` (a path segment ending in `..` with no slash separator, matched by the /[a-z0-9]+\.\. anchor which excludes benign /../ dot-segments) and the encoded `%2e%2e`. Cross-checked against the traefik GHSA advisory and CVE-2026-48020 (StripPrefix, same normalization-bypass class) which confirm both payload variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-48020/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48020/ • https://www.hunt-benito.com/blog/stripprefix-and-the-one-slash-that-broke-auth-cve-2026-48020-traefik-route-level-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Nessus, Burp, Nikto) probing generic path-traversal payloads against the proxy
  • Authorized pentest / red-team engagements against the Traefik entrypoint
  • Legitimate application URLs embedding numeric ranges after a slash, e.g. /api/v1..2/resource
  • Automated crawlers or bots URL-encoding path characters as %2e%2e
  • Broken client that double-appends a relative path producing segment.. artifacts
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop known scanner user-agents while keeping real bypass attempts
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","Nessus","Nmap","masscan","zgrab","Nikto","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits from the same SrcIpAddr; confirm the target DstHostname runs an affected Traefik build (<=2.11.51, <=3.6.22, 3.7.0-3.7.6) and uses ReplacePathRegex without a mandatory slash. Note the HTTP status returned. 2) Contain: if any request returned 2xx, treat as a live bypass — block the source IP at the edge, and hot-patch by upgrading Traefik to 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7 or rewriting the regex to `^/api/(.*)`. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy logs for other auth-gated routes (/admin, /internal, /actuator) reached via `..`/`%2e%2e`, and pivot on the SrcIpAddr for POST/PUT/DELETE traversal attempts indicating write abuse.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has ".." or Url has "%2e%2e" or Url has "%2E%2E" or UrlOriginal has ".." or UrlOriginal has "%2e%2e"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)(/[a-z0-9]+\.\.|%2e%2e)" or UrlOriginal matches regex @"(?i)(/[a-z0-9]+\.\.|%2e%2e)"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-48020/

detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|re: '(?i)(/[a-z0-9]+\.\.|%2e%2e)'
  condition: selection
level: high
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=t allow_old_summaries=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where nodename=Web (Web.url="*..*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.url="*%2E%2E*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.uri_path Web.url Web.status

Traefik auth-bypass confirmed: traversal path returns 2xx on protected route (CVE-2026-65600) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful CVE-2026-65600 exploitation: a request whose path carries a smuggled dot-segment (/api../admin, /api%2e%2e/admin) returns a 2xx from the backend — meaning the un-normalized path resolved past the auth middleware. Write verbs (POST/PUT/DELETE) on such requests indicate unauthenticated data modification, not just read access. Rationale: Refines the CVE-2026-65600 signature to confirmed exploitation by requiring a 2xx response — the article states the backend normalizes /../admin to /admin and returns protected content, so a traversal-path request that succeeds is a high-fidelity bypass. The WriteOp flag isolates POST/PUT/DELETE, the article's explicit impact vector ('Both read and write operations bypass authentication'). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-48020/ • https://www.hunt-benito.com/blog/stripprefix-and-the-one-slash-that-broke-auth-cve-2026-48020-traefik-route-level-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1211 T1213 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vulnerability scanner probe that happens to return 2xx because the backend serves a generic page for the normalized path
  • Legitimate route where the backend intentionally accepts numeric ranges after a slash (e.g. /api/v1..2/) and returns 200
  • A permissive backend returning 200 for all paths (including error pages) inflating perceived success
  • Load-balancer health checks that URL-encode benign characters as %2e
  • Internal QA/automation replaying archived request logs against staging
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: keep confirmed bypasses, drop scanner noise and benign numeric-range paths
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","Nessus","Nmap","masscan","zgrab","Nikto","Burp")
| where not(Url matches regex @"/v?\d+\.\.\d+/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each 2xx hit, inspect the normalized target route — is it an auth-gated endpoint (/admin, /internal, /actuator, config APIs)? Correlate SrcIpAddr against SigninLogs/auth events to confirm NO successful authentication preceded it. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr, upgrade Traefik to 2.11.52/3.6.23/3.7.7 (or add the JoinPath equality check / rewrite regex to `^/api/(.*)`), and rotate any secrets/credentials exposed via the reached admin route. 3) Hunt: enumerate every WriteOp=yes hit (POST/PUT/DELETE) as potential unauthorized data modification; review backend audit logs for state changes from that IP and check for follow-on config tampering or account creation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpStatusCode between (200 .. 299)
| where Url has ".." or Url has "%2e%2e" or Url has "%2E%2E" or UrlOriginal has ".." or UrlOriginal has "%2e%2e"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)(/[a-z0-9]+\.\.|%2e%2e)" or UrlOriginal matches regex @"(?i)(/[a-z0-9]+\.\.|%2e%2e)"
| extend WriteOp = iff(HttpMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH"), "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, WriteOp, HttpStatusCode, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

New Interrupt Injection Attack Can Bypass Spectre v2 Defenses on Intel and AMD CPUs

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 6 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

An unprivileged Linux program can time a hardware interrupt to land in the gap between a processor sanitizing its branch predictor and the kernel using it, re-poisoning the predictor after the defense has run. MIT CSAIL researchers Daniël Trujillo and Mengjia Yan named the technique INTERRUPT INJECTION. On an AMD Zen 2 machine running Linux 6.14 with every default Spectre v2 mitigation on,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

SecurityEvent

description: |

ThreatsDay: Odysseus RCE, Samsung One-Click Takeover, iCloud Backdoor Fight + 27 More Stories

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 20 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Apparently, opening the thing is now enough. A repo can run before the first prompt, a package can hide among hundreds, and a harmless-looking PDF can finish the job. This week runs on cheap leverage: exposed servers, recycled bugs, poisoned agent instructions, remote-access tools dressed as support software, and trusted defaults doing attackers a favor. Nothing here is especially mystical.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SideWinder ClickOnce app + DLL side-load launched from PDF/browser (Apps\2.0) · [LLM] Flooding Dropper npm second-stage: download/write of /pkg/update_win.exe · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Odysseus RCE, Samsung One-Click Takeover, iCloud Backdoor Fight + 27
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Flooding Dropper npm install spawning scheduled task + Run-key persistence · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SideWinder Rust backdoor C2 to Cloudflare Workers (*.workers.dev) from non-browser · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XCSSET v40 Telegram Desktop deletion + malicious replacement (macOS) · [LLM] XCSSET v40 Chrome hijack via Chrome DevTools Protocol remote-debugging port (macOS) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
SideWinder ClickOnce app + DLL side-load launched from PDF/browser (Apps\2.0) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts SideWinder's new infection chain where a phishing PDF's fake 'download Adobe Reader' button retrieves a ClickOnce (.application) package that sideloads an illicit DLL while showing a decoy PDF. Pivots on a process executing from the ClickOnce deployment cache (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Apps\2.0\) with a browser, Acrobat, Outlook or dfsvc.exe parent. Rationale: Trellix and THN's Oct-2025 SideWinder write-up confirm the PDF->fake-Adobe-Reader-button->ClickOnce->DLL-side-load chain; ClickOnce always stages under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Apps\2.0\, and a browser/PDF-reader parent for that path is the article-specific tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/sidewinders-shifting-sands-click-once-for-espionage/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/sidewinder-adopts-new-clickonce-based.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/clickonce-leveraged-in-new-sidewinder-apt-attacks
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate in-house LOB apps distributed via ClickOnce and launched from an intranet portal in a browser
  • Enterprise ClickOnce apps auto-updating via dfsvc.exe on user login
  • IT tooling (remote-support or reporting agents) shipped as ClickOnce
  • Developer testing a ClickOnce deployment from Visual Studio
  • Third-party finance/HR apps that legitimately deploy through Apps\2.0
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dfsvc.exe" and FolderPath has_any ("\\Contoso.LOB\\", "\\YourApprovedClickOnceVendor\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent chain and the .application/manifest URL the ClickOnce app was fetched from; check whether a decoy PDF opened seconds earlier and whether the loaded DLL under Apps\2.0 is unsigned or non-Microsoft. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the ClickOnce process tree, and block the manifest/download domain and any PaaS C2 (workers.dev) at proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep for outbound connections from the Apps\2.0 binary to *.workers.dev and other PaaS domains, and for Run-key persistence written by the same process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Apps\2.0\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dfsvc.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","outlook.exe","AcroRd32.exe","Acrobat.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Apps\2.0\"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("dfsvc.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","AcroRd32.exe","Acrobat.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: SideWinder ClickOnce App Executed From ClickOnce Cache With Browser/PDF Parent

description: Detects a process launched from the ClickOnce deployment cache (Apps\2.0) by a browser, Acrobat, Outlook or dfsvc.exe, matching SideWinder's PDF-lured ClickOnce DLL side-load chain.
references:

  - https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/sidewinders-shifting-sands-click-once-for-espionage/

  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\Apps\\2.0\\* OR *\\apps\\2.0\\*) @ParentImage:(*\\dfsvc.exe OR *\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\outlook.exe OR *\\AcroRd32.exe OR *\\Acrobat.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\AppData\\Local\\Apps\\2\.0\\/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/(dfsvc|chrome|msedge|firefox|outlook|acrord32|acrobat|rundll32)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Apps\\2.0\\*") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("dfsvc.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","AcroRd32.exe","Acrobat.exe","rundll32.exe")) AND NOT (Processes.user IN ("*$")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

SideWinder Rust backdoor C2 to Cloudflare Workers (*.workers.dev) from non-browser AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SideWinder Rust implant's command channel, which uses free serverless PaaS such as Cloudflare Workers. Flags any non-browser process resolving/connecting to a *.workers.dev host, which for a Windows endpoint is almost always the ClickOnce-staged loader rather than a real browser. Rationale: The article and the corroborating SideWinder PaaS-hopping analysis name Cloudflare Workers as the serverless C2; *.workers.dev egress from a non-browser process on a Windows endpoint is a high-signal pairing (the KB flags blanket-trusting workers.dev, so we filter on process instead). Cross-checked against: • https://intel.breakglass.tech/post/sidewinder-20-nodes-8-paas-platforms-mhil-pakistan-defense-dual-password-harvest • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/sidewinders-shifting-sands-click-once-for-espionage/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit SaaS/dev tools (some CLI updaters, Wrangler CLI, Postman) that call an app hosted on workers.dev
  • Corporate apps whose backend/API is deployed on Cloudflare Workers
  • curl/PowerShell used by developers hitting a workers.dev endpoint
  • Security scanners or uptime monitors probing workers.dev assets
  • Electron apps embedding a non-Chrome network stack calling workers.dev
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("wrangler.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Apps\2.0\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary and its path (ClickOnce Apps\2.0 staging = high suspicion), and resolve the exact *.workers.dev subdomain plus request cadence. 2) Contain: block the specific subdomain and, if the process is unsigned/AppData-staged, isolate the host and kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate back to a ClickOnce launch (UC1) on the same host and look for registry Run-key persistence and host-recon commands from the same PID.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".workers.dev"
| where QueryType in ("A","AAAA","HTTPS","")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Non-Browser Process Contacting Cloudflare Workers (workers.dev) C2

Flooding Dropper npm second-stage: download/write of /pkg/update_win.exe AIDelivery High
Hunts the Flooding Dropper npm campaign (Sonatype sonatype-2026-005660) Windows chain, which retrieves an encrypted second stage from a remote '/pkg/update_win.exe' path and reflectively executes it in memory. Pivots on the fixed URL path and the update_win.exe drop. Rationale: Sonatype's Flooding Dropper report gives the exact second-stage path '/pkg/update_win.exe'; a fixed filename + URL path is a near-zero-FP alerting IOC even though the campaign randomizes hosts and lightly mutates the JS loader. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages • https://securityboulevard.com/2026/08/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1620
Data sourcesWeb Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal software-update service that coincidentally names a binary update_win.exe (verify origin URL host)
  • A legitimate vendor patch cache placing update_win.exe under Program Files rather than AppData/Temp
  • Security-team detonation of the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • Proxy log replay/testing that reissues archived URLs
  • A dev mirror proxy caching third-party update paths
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\") or isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the download host and the initiating process (node.exe/npm during an install = confirmation of the npm vector); capture the update_win.exe hash and AppData copy location. 2) Contain: quarantine update_win.exe, isolate the host, and block the download host/IP; audit package.json/lockfile for packages with bigops/bnpl names or 35.x.y versions and purge them. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a scheduled task + HKCU Run key created post-install (UC4) and any child that patched ETW/AMSI before beaconing.
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "/pkg/update_win.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "update_win.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, FileOriginUrl, SHA256;
union NetHits, FileHits
| order by Timestamp desc

Flooding Dropper npm install spawning scheduled task + Run-key persistence AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence stage of Flooding Dropper: a Windows npm install (node.exe/npm) leads to a scheduled task creation and an HKCU Run-key write for the copied AppData loader. Pivots on node/npm parentage of schtasks.exe /create or reg add ...\CurrentVersion\Run. Rationale: Sonatype confirms Flooding Dropper's Windows loader establishes persistence via BOTH a Registry Run key and a scheduled task after copying itself to AppData; anchoring on node/npm parentage keeps this narrow to the malicious-package install vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages • https://securityboulevard.com/2026/08/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • postinstall scripts of legitimate npm packages that register a scheduled task (some updater/electron tooling)
  • Developer tooling that writes an HKCU Run entry for a tray helper during npm install
  • CI/CD build agents running npm that configure scheduled tasks as part of provisioning
  • node-based installers for legit desktop apps (VS Code extension build steps)
  • Corporate managed-install wrappers invoking npm then scheduling maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("YourApprovedUpdater", "CorpMaintenanceTask") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the schtasks /create and Run-key values to recover the persisted binary path (expect an AppData-copied loader), and confirm the triggering package name/version (bigops/bnpl, 35.x.y). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task and Run value, quarantine the AppData binary, isolate the host, and remove the offending npm package + clean the lockfile. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 for the update_win.exe fetch and to network logs for post-persistence beaconing; sweep other dev hosts that installed the same package.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd")
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create")
     or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has @"CurrentVersion\Run")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"CurrentVersion\Run")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "CurrentVersion\\Run")
     or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "CurrentVersion\\Run")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

XCSSET v40 Telegram Desktop deletion + malicious replacement (macOS) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts XCSSET v40's Telegram trojanizer, which deletes the legitimate Telegram Desktop app and drops a malicious replacement to intercept communications. Pivots on delete/create activity against Telegram.app initiated by a process that is not the Telegram installer or the app itself. Rationale: Unit 42 (via THN and BleepingComputer) confirms XCSSET v40's Telegram trojanizer deletes the legitimate Telegram Desktop and substitutes a malicious build; delete+create of Telegram.app by a non-installer process is the article-specific host signal. Datadog/CloudWatch empty — macOS EDR telemetry not in those pipelines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-xcsset-variant-targets-macos-devs-via-compromised-xcode-projects/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/
ATT&CKT1554 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User uninstalling then reinstalling Telegram via the App Store or DMG (installd/launchd should be the actor)
  • A managed-software tool (Jamf/Munki) upgrading Telegram Desktop
  • Homebrew cask upgrade of telegram replacing the .app bundle
  • User manually dragging Telegram.app to Trash then reinstalling
  • Backup/restore software rewriting the app bundle
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Munki","jamf","brew","installer") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/usr/local/Caskroom/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/parent that deleted Telegram.app (Xcode/build-agent or an AppData-staged binary points to XCSSET), and hash the replacement bundle to compare against the notarized Telegram build. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, remove the malicious Telegram.app, and reinstall from the official notarized source; check for the fileless loader in memory. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC6), infected Xcode projects, and worm-spread to other local Xcode projects/GitHub repos.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "Telegram.app" or PreviousFolderPath has "Telegram.app"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","installd","system_installd","Install Telegram","launchd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "Telegram.app"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","installd","system_installd","launchd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 Chrome hijack via Chrome DevTools Protocol remote-debugging port (macOS) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts XCSSET v40's Chrome hijacker, which wraps Chrome in a malicious launcher and enables the Chrome DevTools Protocol on a local port to fetch attacker JS and steal cookies/credentials/MetaMask transactions. Pivots on Chrome (or a wrapper) launched with --remote-debugging-port, which is abnormal for user-driven browsing. Rationale: Cybersecurity News and BleepingComputer confirm XCSSET v40 enables the Chrome DevTools Protocol via a local port to fetch C2 JavaScript and steal cookies/credentials/MetaMask data; a Chrome process started with --remote-debugging-port is a rare, high-signal indicator of CDP abuse. Datadog/CloudWatch empty — macOS EDR telemetry not in those pipelines. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-xcsset-variant-targets-macos-devs-via-compromised-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1185 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running headless Chrome automation (Puppeteer, Playwright, Selenium) that legitimately sets --remote-debugging-port
  • Web-scraping or synthetic-monitoring tooling driving Chrome via CDP
  • Electron app debugging sessions
  • Security researchers using CDP for analysis
  • CI browser-test runners on developer laptops
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node","node.exe","Playwright","chromedriver","Puppeteer") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/node_modules/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent of the CDP-enabled Chrome — a wrapper/launcher from AppData or an unsigned bundle (vs puppeteer/playwright node parent) signals XCSSET; note the debugging port and any local process connecting to it. 2) Contain: kill the wrapper and Chrome, isolate the host, and force cookie/session invalidation + password resets for high-value accounts (incl. crypto/MetaMask). 3) Hunt: correlate with the Telegram trojanizer (UC5), infected Xcode projects, and outbound C2 fetching JS; review browser sessions for injected JS and anomalous transaction redirects.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Chrome" or FileName has_any ("Google Chrome","chrome")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Chrome"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

Over 4,400 Rockwell PLCs Exposed Online, 22 Found in Water Attack Cities

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 7 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Forescout found 22 internet-facing Rockwell Automation programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in cities hit by recent cyberattacks on US water utilities. Nineteen used the same mobile carrier network. Its August 3 scan counted 4,407 exposed Rockwell controllers worldwide, including 2,844 in the United States, but Forescout could not confirm any were compromised. That figure counts exposed
